problems.title: Number each user's tweets
problems.statement_md: A Twitter-style app wants to label every tweet with its position in that account's own timeline of posts: 1 for the account's first tweet, 2 for its second, and so on. Order by `posted_on`; when an account tweeted several times on the same day, the lower `tweet_id` comes first. Return `user_id`, `tweet_id`, `posted_on`, `tweet_seq`, ordered by `user_id`, then `tweet_seq`.

tables.name: tweets
tables.description_md: One row per tweet. An account can tweet several times on the same day.

hints_md: The numbering has to restart for every account.
Two tweets on the same day must still get different numbers, so the sort inside the window needs a second key.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Numbering rows inside a group. Interviewers open with it to check that you know PARTITION BY and why a tie-breaker matters.

**Shape:** Split the rows into one group per account, sort each group by date then id, and hand out 1, 2, 3 in that order. Nothing is collapsed: every tweet stays a row.

**Syntax:** `ROW_NUMBER()` takes no argument and gives every row in its partition a distinct number following the window's ORDER BY. Without PARTITION BY the whole result is one partition.

**Trap:** Sorting only by date leaves same-day tweets in an arbitrary order, so the numbering can change between runs. A ranking function that lets equal dates share a number is also not a sequence.

**Interview follow-up:** How would you number the tweets without a window function? (Count the rows of the same account that sort before this one.)

solutions.label: ROW_NUMBER
solutions.explain_md: ROW_NUMBER restarts per account and, with tweet_id as the second sort key, never repeats a number.
solutions.sql:
SELECT user_id, tweet_id, posted_on,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY posted_on, tweet_id) AS tweet_seq
FROM tweets
ORDER BY user_id, tweet_seq;

solutions.label: Correlated count
solutions.explain_md: The position of a tweet is the number of the same account's tweets that sort at or before it.
solutions.sql:
SELECT t.user_id, t.tweet_id, t.posted_on,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tweets x
        WHERE x.user_id = t.user_id
          AND (x.posted_on < t.posted_on OR (x.posted_on = t.posted_on AND x.tweet_id <= t.tweet_id))) AS tweet_seq
FROM tweets t
ORDER BY t.user_id, tweet_seq;

traps.explain_md: RANK gives both same-day tweets the same number, so the sequence has a repeat.
traps.sql:
SELECT user_id, tweet_id, posted_on,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY posted_on) AS tweet_seq
FROM tweets
ORDER BY user_id, tweet_seq, tweet_id;

traps.explain_md: Without PARTITION BY the numbering runs across all accounts instead of restarting.
traps.sql:
SELECT user_id, tweet_id, posted_on,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY user_id, posted_on, tweet_id) AS tweet_seq
FROM tweets
ORDER BY user_id, tweet_seq;

problems.title: Three ways to rank a chart
problems.statement_md: A Spotify-style music service is arguing about how to display its weekly top-tracks chart. For every track, show three position columns side by side, ordered by `streams` descending: `row_no` (every track gets a different position; equal streams are separated alphabetically by `track`), `rank_pos` (equal streams share a position and the next position is skipped), and `dense_pos` (equal streams share a position and the next position is not skipped). Return `track`, `streams`, `row_no`, `rank_pos`, `dense_pos`, ordered by `row_no`.

tables.name: weekly_chart
tables.description_md: One row per track with this week's stream count (thousands).

hints_md: Each of the three columns is a different ranking function over the same ordering.
Look at what happens after a group of tied tracks: one column continues counting rows, one jumps ahead, one just goes to the next number.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** The three ranking functions compared. A classic warm-up: the interviewer asks what each does on ties.

**Shape:** One query, one ordering, three function calls. The differences show only where streams repeat.

**Syntax:** `ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()` take no arguments; all need `OVER (ORDER BY ...)`. Tied rows are peers: they get the same value from RANK and DENSE_RANK, never from ROW_NUMBER.

**Trap:** Using one function for all three columns, or forgetting the second sort key so the numbering of tied rows is unstable.

**Interview follow-up:** When would you pick each? (Unique id: ROW_NUMBER. Olympic-style places: RANK. Levels or Nth distinct value: DENSE_RANK.)

solutions.label: Three window functions
solutions.explain_md: All three share the same ordering; only their tie handling differs.
solutions.sql:
SELECT track, streams,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY streams DESC, track) AS row_no,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY streams DESC) AS rank_pos,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY streams DESC) AS dense_pos
FROM weekly_chart
ORDER BY row_no;

solutions.label: Correlated counts
solutions.explain_md: Each position is a count of tracks that beat this one: rows ahead, strictly better rows, or distinct better stream counts.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.track, c.streams,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM weekly_chart x WHERE x.streams > c.streams OR (x.streams = c.streams AND x.track <= c.track)) AS row_no,
       1 + (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM weekly_chart x WHERE x.streams > c.streams) AS rank_pos,
       1 + (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT x.streams) FROM weekly_chart x WHERE x.streams > c.streams) AS dense_pos
FROM weekly_chart c
ORDER BY row_no;

traps.explain_md: Using RANK for every column makes row_no repeat on ties instead of being unique.
traps.sql:
SELECT track, streams,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY streams DESC) AS row_no,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY streams DESC) AS rank_pos,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY streams DESC) AS dense_pos
FROM weekly_chart
ORDER BY row_no, track;

problems.title: Gold, silver, bronze per challenge
problems.statement_md: An Instagram-style app runs themed reel challenges and awards badges by `likes`. The best like count in a challenge wins gold, the next-best count silver, the next bronze, and creators with exactly the same count get the same badge: if two creators tie for gold, the next distinct count still earns silver. Return `challenge`, `creator`, `likes`, `medal` for every badge winner, ordered by `challenge`, then `likes` descending, then `creator`.

tables.name: reels
tables.description_md: One row per challenge entry (likes in thousands).

hints_md: Think about what the rank should be for the creator who follows a tied pair.
Compute the rank first, then filter on it in an outer query; a window function cannot be used directly in WHERE.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Top 3 by distinct level, ties sharing a level. Interviewers use it to separate RANK from DENSE_RANK.

**Shape:** Rank entries inside each challenge with a ranking that never skips numbers, then keep the first three levels and translate the level into a badge name.

**Syntax:** `DENSE_RANK()` numbers distinct values 1, 2, 3 with no gaps. `CASE n WHEN 1 THEN 'x' ... END` maps numbers to labels.

**Trap:** RANK skips numbers after a tie, so the creator after a tied pair is rank 3 or worse and silently loses a badge level.

**Interview follow-up:** How would you award at most three badges per challenge regardless of ties? (Switch to ROW_NUMBER and choose a tie-break.)

solutions.label: DENSE_RANK + CASE
solutions.explain_md: DENSE_RANK has no gaps, so level 1, 2 and 3 are the three best distinct like counts.
solutions.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT challenge, creator, likes,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY challenge ORDER BY likes DESC) AS lvl
  FROM reels
)
SELECT challenge, creator, likes,
       CASE lvl WHEN 1 THEN 'Gold' WHEN 2 THEN 'Silver' ELSE 'Bronze' END AS medal
FROM ranked
WHERE lvl <= 3
ORDER BY challenge, likes DESC, creator;

solutions.label: Count distinct better counts
solutions.explain_md: The level is one plus the number of distinct higher like counts in the same challenge.
solutions.sql:
SELECT challenge, creator, likes,
       CASE lvl WHEN 1 THEN 'Gold' WHEN 2 THEN 'Silver' ELSE 'Bronze' END AS medal
FROM (
  SELECT r.challenge, r.creator, r.likes,
         1 + (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT x.likes) FROM reels x WHERE x.challenge = r.challenge AND x.likes > r.likes) AS lvl
  FROM reels r
) t
WHERE lvl <= 3
ORDER BY challenge, likes DESC, creator;

traps.explain_md: RANK jumps from 1 straight to 3 after a tie, so the next-best creator after tied leaders is cut and a level is mislabelled.
traps.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT challenge, creator, likes,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY challenge ORDER BY likes DESC) AS lvl
  FROM reels
)
SELECT challenge, creator, likes,
       CASE lvl WHEN 1 THEN 'Gold' WHEN 2 THEN 'Silver' ELSE 'Bronze' END AS medal
FROM ranked
WHERE lvl <= 3
ORDER BY challenge, likes DESC, creator;

problems.title: Top two earning channels per category
problems.statement_md: A YouTube-style partner team wants the two best-earning channels in every content category, but ties must be handled fairly. Return every channel that has at most one higher-earning channel in the same category: tied channels are all returned (so a category can return more than two channels), yet nobody is returned just because the channels above them are tied. Return `category`, `channel`, `monthly_revenue`, ordered by `category`, then `monthly_revenue` descending, then `channel`.

tables.name: channel_earnings
tables.description_md: One row per channel with its monthly ad revenue.

hints_md: Translate 'at most one higher-earning channel' into a rank number and decide which ranking function produces it.
Check Gaming and Cooking: look at what each ranking function does to the third channel when the top two (or second and third) tie.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Top N per group with ties kept. The standard follow-up to 'highest earner per group'.

**Shape:** Rank channels within their category by revenue, keep ranks up to N in an outer query. The ranking function is the whole decision: it must say how many channels are strictly better.

**Syntax:** `RANK()` is 1 + the number of rows strictly ahead, so `RANK() <= 2` means at most one strictly better row. `DENSE_RANK()` counts distinct revenue levels instead; `ROW_NUMBER()` ignores ties.

**Trap:** ROW_NUMBER cuts one of two tied channels at the boundary; DENSE_RANK lets a third channel in when the top two tie.

**Interview follow-up:** What if the business wanted the top two distinct revenue levels instead? (DENSE_RANK <= 2.)

solutions.label: RANK
solutions.explain_md: RANK equals 1 plus the number of strictly higher revenues, so RANK <= 2 is exactly 'at most one higher-earning channel'.
solutions.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT category, channel, monthly_revenue,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY monthly_revenue DESC) AS rnk
  FROM channel_earnings
)
SELECT category, channel, monthly_revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 2
ORDER BY category, monthly_revenue DESC, channel;

solutions.label: Correlated count
solutions.explain_md: Count the channels in the same category that earn strictly more and keep those with fewer than two.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.category, c.channel, c.monthly_revenue
FROM channel_earnings c
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM channel_earnings x WHERE x.category = c.category AND x.monthly_revenue > c.monthly_revenue) < 2
ORDER BY c.category, c.monthly_revenue DESC, c.channel;

traps.explain_md: ROW_NUMBER always returns exactly two rows per category, so one of two tied channels is dropped.
traps.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT category, channel, monthly_revenue,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY monthly_revenue DESC, channel) AS rn
  FROM channel_earnings
)
SELECT category, channel, monthly_revenue FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY category, monthly_revenue DESC, channel;

traps.explain_md: DENSE_RANK counts revenue levels, so when the top two tie it also lets in the next channel.
traps.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT category, channel, monthly_revenue,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY monthly_revenue DESC) AS rnk
  FROM channel_earnings
)
SELECT category, channel, monthly_revenue FROM ranked WHERE rnk <= 2
ORDER BY category, monthly_revenue DESC, channel;

problems.title: Third-highest distinct fare
problems.statement_md: An Uber-style pricing team wants the third-highest distinct fare ever charged, counting each fare amount once no matter how many rides cost that much. Cancelled rides have no fare (`NULL`) and are not a fare level. Return a single row with the column `third_highest_fare`; it must be `NULL` if fewer than three distinct fares exist.

tables.name: ride_fares
tables.description_md: One row per ride. `fare` is NULL for cancelled rides.

hints_md: Duplicates must not use up a position: the highest fare appears twice.
Whatever you build must still return one row, with a NULL, when the position does not exist.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Nth highest distinct value. A perennial interview question, usually with the 'what if it does not exist' twist.

**Shape:** Rank the distinct fare levels from the top, pick the level numbered N, and make sure an empty pick still yields one NULL row instead of no rows.

**Syntax:** `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY x DESC)` numbers distinct values with no gaps. `MAX(x)` over zero rows returns NULL, which makes a handy 'one row or NULL' wrapper. `LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2` skips two rows, not two distinct values.

**Trap:** ROW_NUMBER or a plain OFFSET counts duplicate fares as separate positions and returns the wrong level.

**Interview follow-up:** How would you generalise to the Nth distinct value per city? (Add PARTITION BY city to the ranking.)

solutions.label: DENSE_RANK + MAX
solutions.explain_md: DENSE_RANK numbers the distinct fares; MAX over the matching row turns 'no row' into NULL.
solutions.sql:
SELECT MAX(fare) AS third_highest_fare
FROM (
  SELECT fare, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY fare DESC) AS rnk
  FROM ride_fares
  WHERE fare IS NOT NULL
) t
WHERE rnk = 3;

solutions.label: DISTINCT + OFFSET in a scalar subquery
solutions.explain_md: A scalar subquery that finds no row evaluates to NULL, giving the required fallback.
solutions.sql:
SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT fare FROM ride_fares
        WHERE fare IS NOT NULL
        ORDER BY fare DESC
        LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2) AS third_highest_fare;

traps.explain_md: ROW_NUMBER counts the duplicate 40.00 and 35.50 rides as separate positions and returns 35.50.
traps.sql:
SELECT MAX(fare) AS third_highest_fare
FROM (
  SELECT fare, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY fare DESC) AS rn
  FROM ride_fares
  WHERE fare IS NOT NULL
) t
WHERE rn = 3;

traps.explain_md: OFFSET without DISTINCT skips two rides, not two fare levels.
traps.sql:
SELECT (SELECT fare FROM ride_fares
        WHERE fare IS NOT NULL
        ORDER BY fare DESC
        LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2) AS third_highest_fare;

problems.title: Keep the latest record per email
problems.statement_md: An Outlook-style address book has been synced from several devices, so the same contact exists in several saved versions, one row per sync. Keep only the most recent version of each `email` (latest `modified_at`). If two versions of an email share the same `modified_at`, keep the one with the higher `contact_id`. Return `contact_id`, `email`, `display_name`, `modified_at`, ordered by `email`.

tables.name: address_book
tables.description_md: One row per saved version of a contact.

hints_md: You need whole rows back, not just the latest date, so a plain GROUP BY on email is not enough.
Number the versions inside each email from newest to oldest, with a tie-breaker, and keep number one.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Deduplication: one row per key, newest wins. The most common practical use of a window function.

**Shape:** Order each email's rows newest first (id breaks exact ties), number them, and keep only the first.

**Syntax:** `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY t DESC)` numbers the rows of each partition 1, 2, 3 in that order, so exactly one row per partition is number 1. A window result must be filtered in an outer query or CTE.

**Trap:** Joining back to MAX(modified_at) keeps every row that shares the latest timestamp, so exact ties return two rows.

**Interview follow-up:** How would you delete the old versions instead of selecting the new ones? (Delete rows whose number is greater than 1, or rows that have a newer sibling.)

solutions.label: ROW_NUMBER
solutions.explain_md: Exactly one row per email gets number 1, even when timestamps tie, because contact_id breaks the tie.
solutions.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT contact_id, email, display_name, modified_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY modified_at DESC, contact_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM address_book
)
SELECT contact_id, email, display_name, modified_at
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY email;

solutions.label: NOT EXISTS a newer version
solutions.explain_md: A row survives when no other version of the same email is newer, or equally new with a higher id.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.contact_id, c.email, c.display_name, c.modified_at
FROM address_book c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM address_book x
  WHERE x.email = c.email
    AND (x.modified_at > c.modified_at OR (x.modified_at = c.modified_at AND x.contact_id > c.contact_id))
)
ORDER BY c.email;

traps.explain_md: Joining to the per-email MAX(modified_at) returns both versions when two share the latest timestamp.
traps.sql:
SELECT c.contact_id, c.email, c.display_name, c.modified_at
FROM address_book c
JOIN (SELECT email, MAX(modified_at) AS latest FROM address_book GROUP BY email) m
  ON m.email = c.email AND m.latest = c.modified_at
ORDER BY c.email, c.contact_id;

problems.title: First title each profile watched
problems.statement_md: A Netflix-style streaming company studies how new profiles start. For every profile, find the first viewing session it ever had and which title was watched in it. When a profile watched several titles on its first day, take the session with the lowest `view_id`. Return `profile_id`, `view_id`, `watched_on`, `title`, with exactly one row per profile, ordered by `profile_id`.

tables.name: watch_history
tables.description_md: One row per viewing session. A profile can watch several titles on one day.

hints_md: Finding each profile's earliest date is easy; the difficulty is getting exactly one row when two sessions share it.
Number each profile's sessions in the order that defines 'first', then keep number one.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** First row per group (earliest event). A cousin of top-N-per-group with N = 1.

**Shape:** Number every profile's sessions from earliest to latest with an explicit tie-break and keep the first one.

**Syntax:** `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY d, id)` numbers each partition's rows in the order given, so number 1 is the first one. `MIN(d)` returns only the date, never the rest of the row.

**Trap:** Joining back on the earliest date returns every session on that date, so a same-day tie yields two rows for one profile.

**Interview follow-up:** How would you solve it without a window function? (NOT EXISTS an earlier session, with the id as tie-break.)

solutions.label: ROW_NUMBER
solutions.explain_md: With the id as second sort key every profile has exactly one row numbered 1.
solutions.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT profile_id, view_id, watched_on, title,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY profile_id ORDER BY watched_on, view_id) AS rn
  FROM watch_history
)
SELECT profile_id, view_id, watched_on, title
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY profile_id;

solutions.label: NOT EXISTS an earlier session
solutions.explain_md: A session is the first one when no other session of that profile comes before it by date, or by id on the same date.
solutions.sql:
SELECT w.profile_id, w.view_id, w.watched_on, w.title
FROM watch_history w
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM watch_history x
  WHERE x.profile_id = w.profile_id
    AND (x.watched_on < w.watched_on OR (x.watched_on = w.watched_on AND x.view_id < w.view_id))
)
ORDER BY w.profile_id;

traps.explain_md: Joining to MIN(watched_on) returns both sessions from a shared first day.
traps.sql:
SELECT w.profile_id, w.view_id, w.watched_on, w.title
FROM watch_history w
JOIN (SELECT profile_id, MIN(watched_on) AS first_day FROM watch_history GROUP BY profile_id) f
  ON f.profile_id = w.profile_id AND f.first_day = w.watched_on
ORDER BY w.profile_id, w.view_id;

problems.title: Rank products by revenue within department
problems.statement_md: An Amazon-style marketplace wants every product placed in its department's revenue league table. Revenue of a product is the sum of `units * unit_price` over all its order lines. Position 1 is the highest revenue; products with identical revenue share a position and the following position is skipped. Return `department`, `product`, `revenue`, `department_rank`, ordered by `department`, then `department_rank`, then `product`.
hints_md: There are two levels here: first one row per product, then a ranking of those rows.
A window function runs after GROUP BY, so it can order by an aggregate in the same SELECT, or you can aggregate in a CTE first.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Ranking an aggregate. Tests whether you know the order of evaluation: GROUP BY, then window functions, then ORDER BY.

**Shape:** Collapse order lines into one row per product with a revenue sum, then rank those rows inside each department. It can be one query or a CTE followed by a ranking query.

**Syntax:** A ranking function's ORDER BY may use an aggregate such as `SUM(x)` in a grouped query: windows are evaluated after GROUP BY and HAVING and see the grouped rows.

**Trap:** Ranking raw lines before aggregating, forgetting PARTITION BY (one league table for the whole store), or using ROW_NUMBER so tied products get different positions.

**Interview follow-up:** How would you show only the top product per department, ties included? (Rank in a CTE and filter rank = 1.)

solutions.label: Window over the grouped result
solutions.explain_md: Window functions run after GROUP BY, so the ranking can order by the SUM of each product.
solutions.sql:
SELECT department, product,
       SUM(units * unit_price) AS revenue,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY SUM(units * unit_price) DESC) AS department_rank
FROM order_lines
GROUP BY department, product
ORDER BY department, department_rank, product;

solutions.label: CTE then rank
solutions.explain_md: Aggregate first so the ranking works on plain columns.
solutions.sql:
WITH totals AS (
  SELECT department, product, SUM(units * unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM order_lines
  GROUP BY department, product
)
SELECT department, product, revenue,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS department_rank
FROM totals
ORDER BY department, department_rank, product;

traps.explain_md: Without PARTITION BY the products are ranked in one store-wide table, so positions in Electronics continue after Books.
traps.sql:
SELECT department, product,
       SUM(units * unit_price) AS revenue,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(units * unit_price) DESC) AS department_rank
FROM order_lines
GROUP BY department, product
ORDER BY department, department_rank, product;

traps.explain_md: ROW_NUMBER gives the two tied Electronics products different positions.
traps.sql:
SELECT department, product,
       SUM(units * unit_price) AS revenue,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY SUM(units * unit_price) DESC, product) AS department_rank
FROM order_lines
GROUP BY department, product
ORDER BY department, department_rank, product;

problems.title: Leaderboard movers
problems.statement_md: An Xbox-style achievements service publishes a weekly leaderboard by `gamerscore` earned that week (highest first; equal scores share a position and the next position is skipped). Each week's position counts everyone who scored that week. For gamertags that appear in both week 1 and week 2, return `gamertag`, `rank_week1`, `rank_week2` and `positions_gained` (week 1 position minus week 2 position, so a positive number means they climbed). Order by `positions_gained` descending, then `gamertag`.

tables.name: weekly_gamerscore
tables.description_md: One row per gamertag per week they were active.

hints_md: Each week has its own league table: the ranking must restart for every week.
Rank first using everyone who played that week; only afterwards drop gamertags that are missing from one of the weeks.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Rank in two periods, then compare. Typical of 'biggest movers' questions.

**Shape:** Rank every row within its week, then bring the two weeks side by side for each gamertag (self-join or conditional aggregation) and subtract.

**Syntax:** `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY week_no ORDER BY score DESC)` restarts per week. `MAX(CASE WHEN week_no = 1 THEN rnk END)` picks one week's value out of a group.

**Trap:** Filtering to players present in both weeks before ranking changes everybody's position, because the positions are published for the whole field. Forgetting PARTITION BY ranks both weeks as one list.

**Interview follow-up:** How would you also list players who dropped out or newly joined? (Use a full outer comparison and show NULL for the missing week.)

solutions.label: Rank per week, then self-join
solutions.explain_md: The CTE ranks each week on its own; joining week 1 to week 2 on the gamertag drops anyone missing from either week.
solutions.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT gamertag, week_no,
         CAST(RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY week_no ORDER BY gamerscore DESC) AS SIGNED) AS rnk
  FROM weekly_gamerscore
)
SELECT a.gamertag, a.rnk AS rank_week1, b.rnk AS rank_week2, a.rnk - b.rnk AS positions_gained
FROM ranked a
JOIN ranked b ON b.gamertag = a.gamertag AND b.week_no = 2
WHERE a.week_no = 1
ORDER BY positions_gained DESC, a.gamertag;

solutions.label: Conditional aggregation
solutions.explain_md: Group the ranked rows by gamertag and pick out each week's rank; HAVING keeps gamertags that have both.
solutions.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT gamertag, week_no,
         CAST(RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY week_no ORDER BY gamerscore DESC) AS SIGNED) AS rnk
  FROM weekly_gamerscore
)
SELECT gamertag,
       MAX(CASE WHEN week_no = 1 THEN rnk END) AS rank_week1,
       MAX(CASE WHEN week_no = 2 THEN rnk END) AS rank_week2,
       MAX(CASE WHEN week_no = 1 THEN rnk END) - MAX(CASE WHEN week_no = 2 THEN rnk END) AS positions_gained
FROM ranked
GROUP BY gamertag
HAVING COUNT(*) = 2
ORDER BY positions_gained DESC, gamertag;

traps.explain_md: Without PARTITION BY both weeks are ranked as one combined list, so the positions are wrong.
traps.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT gamertag, week_no,
         CAST(RANK() OVER (ORDER BY gamerscore DESC) AS SIGNED) AS rnk
  FROM weekly_gamerscore
)
SELECT a.gamertag, a.rnk AS rank_week1, b.rnk AS rank_week2, a.rnk - b.rnk AS positions_gained
FROM ranked a
JOIN ranked b ON b.gamertag = a.gamertag AND b.week_no = 2
WHERE a.week_no = 1
ORDER BY positions_gained DESC, a.gamertag;

traps.explain_md: Dropping gamertags absent from a week before ranking shifts everyone's position in the published table.
traps.sql:
WITH both_weeks AS (
  SELECT * FROM weekly_gamerscore
  WHERE gamertag IN (SELECT gamertag FROM weekly_gamerscore WHERE week_no = 1)
    AND gamertag IN (SELECT gamertag FROM weekly_gamerscore WHERE week_no = 2)
), ranked AS (
  SELECT gamertag, week_no,
         CAST(RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY week_no ORDER BY gamerscore DESC) AS SIGNED) AS rnk
  FROM both_weeks
)
SELECT a.gamertag, a.rnk AS rank_week1, b.rnk AS rank_week2, a.rnk - b.rnk AS positions_gained
FROM ranked a
JOIN ranked b ON b.gamertag = a.gamertag AND b.week_no = 2
WHERE a.week_no = 1
ORDER BY positions_gained DESC, a.gamertag;

problems.dialect_note_md: In MySQL a ranking function returns an unsigned integer, so subtracting a larger rank from a smaller one raises an out-of-range error instead of going negative.

problems.title: Split creators into follower tiers
problems.statement_md: An Instagram-style creator programme has 12 accounts and wants four tiers of equal size: tier 1 is the quarter with the most followers, tier 4 the quarter with the fewest. Sort by `followers` descending; accounts with the same follower count are ordered by `account_id`. Return `account_id`, `handle`, `followers`, `tier`, ordered by `followers` descending, then `account_id`.

tables.name: creator_accounts
tables.description_md: One row per creator account (followers in thousands).

hints_md: You are cutting an ordered list into equal slices, not grouping by value.
Two accounts share 245 thousand followers; the secondary sort key decides which of them goes into which tier.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Equal-size buckets (quartiles, deciles, tiers). Come up whenever the question says 'top 25%' or 'split into n groups'.

**Shape:** Order the rows, then let the database cut the ordered list into n consecutive slices and label them 1..n.

**Syntax:** `NTILE(n) OVER (ORDER BY k)` takes the number of buckets n and numbers them 1 to n in the order given. Add a second sort key so ties are cut deterministically.

**Trap:** Ordering ascending flips which tier is 'first'; ordering by a non-unique key makes the cut through tied rows unstable.

**Interview follow-up:** What if the count does not divide evenly? (See the next drill on uneven buckets.)

solutions.label: NTILE
solutions.explain_md: NTILE(4) cuts the ordered list into four equal slices numbered from 1.
solutions.sql:
SELECT account_id, handle, followers,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY followers DESC, account_id) AS tier
FROM creator_accounts
ORDER BY followers DESC, account_id;

solutions.label: ROW_NUMBER arithmetic
solutions.explain_md: With 12 rows, 3 accounts fit in each tier, so the tier is the row position scaled by the tier count and total, rounded up.
solutions.sql:
SELECT account_id, handle, followers,
       CEIL(ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY followers DESC, account_id) * 4 / COUNT(*) OVER ()) AS tier
FROM creator_accounts
ORDER BY followers DESC, account_id;

traps.explain_md: Sorting ascending numbers the smallest accounts as tier 1, reversing the tiers.
traps.sql:
SELECT account_id, handle, followers,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY followers, account_id) AS tier
FROM creator_accounts
ORDER BY followers DESC, account_id;

problems.title: Uneven buckets
problems.statement_md: A Microsoft Teams-style support channel answered 10 questions. Sort them from fastest to slowest by `reply_minutes` (the time to the first reply; `question_id` breaks ties) and cut that list into 3 consecutive groups numbered 1 to 3. When the questions cannot be split evenly, the earlier groups receive the extra questions. For each group return `bucket`, `questions` (how many), `fastest_minutes` and `slowest_minutes`, ordered by `bucket`.
hints_md: Work out by hand how 10 rows split into 3 groups before writing anything, and which groups get the leftover row.
You need the bucket number per question first, then an aggregate per bucket.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Uneven bucketing and per-bucket summaries. Tests whether you know how the database spreads the remainder.

**Shape:** Label every question with its bucket in a CTE, then group by the bucket and take count, min and max.

**Syntax:** With `NTILE(n)`, if the rows divide into n groups with a remainder r, the first r buckets get one extra row each. Window functions cannot be used inside GROUP BY, so label first, aggregate second.

**Trap:** Assuming the extra rows land in the last bucket (as a hand-rolled CEIL formula would put them), or trying to aggregate and number in the same SELECT.

**Interview follow-up:** How do you build the same buckets by value range instead of by row count? (Width-based buckets with a CASE or arithmetic on the value.)

solutions.label: NTILE in a CTE
solutions.explain_md: NTILE(3) over 10 rows gives sizes 4, 3, 3; grouping the labelled rows summarises each bucket.
solutions.sql:
WITH tiled AS (
  SELECT question_id, reply_minutes,
         NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY reply_minutes, question_id) AS bucket
  FROM channel_questions
)
SELECT bucket,
       COUNT(*) AS questions,
       MIN(reply_minutes) AS fastest_minutes,
       MAX(reply_minutes) AS slowest_minutes
FROM tiled
GROUP BY bucket
ORDER BY bucket;

traps.explain_md: A hand-rolled formula that rounds the position up puts the extra question in the last bucket (3, 3, 4) instead of the first.
traps.sql:
WITH tiled AS (
  SELECT question_id, reply_minutes,
         CEIL(ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY reply_minutes, question_id) * 3 / COUNT(*) OVER ()) AS bucket
  FROM channel_questions
)
SELECT bucket,
       COUNT(*) AS questions,
       MIN(reply_minutes) AS fastest_minutes,
       MAX(reply_minutes) AS slowest_minutes
FROM tiled
GROUP BY bucket
ORDER BY bucket;

problems.title: Price percentile within city
problems.statement_md: An Airbnb-style host-tools team shows each listing where its nightly price sits within its own city, defined as the percentage of the city's *other* listings that are strictly cheaper, rounded to one decimal. The cheapest listing scores 0 and the dearest 100; a city with a single listing scores 0. Return `city`, `title`, `nightly_price`, `price_percentile`, ordered by `city`, then `nightly_price`, then `title`.
hints_md: Note the exact definition: strictly cheaper, and divided by the other listings, not by all of them.
Listings with the same price must get the same percentile, and a one-listing city must not divide by zero.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Percentile position of each row. Shows up as 'where does this value sit in its group'.

**Shape:** Order each city by price ascending and let a distribution function report the relative standing, then scale to a percentage and round.

**Syntax:** `PERCENT_RANK()` = (rank - 1) / (rows in partition - 1), always between 0 and 1, and 0 for a one-row partition. `CUME_DIST()` is a different quantity: rows up to and including this one divided by all rows.

**Trap:** Using CUME_DIST (never 0, counts ties as 'at or below') or dividing the count of cheaper listings by the full city size.

**Interview follow-up:** How would you compute the same number without PERCENT_RANK? (Count strictly cheaper listings in the city and divide by size minus one, guarding the one-row case.)

solutions.label: PERCENT_RANK
solutions.explain_md: PERCENT_RANK is exactly the share of other rows that sort strictly before the current peer group.
solutions.sql:
SELECT city, title, nightly_price,
       ROUND(PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY nightly_price) * 100, 1) AS price_percentile
FROM listings
ORDER BY city, nightly_price, title;

solutions.label: Correlated counts
solutions.explain_md: Count the strictly cheaper listings and divide by the city size minus one; NULLIF avoids dividing by zero and COALESCE turns that case into 0.
solutions.sql:
SELECT l.city, l.title, l.nightly_price,
       COALESCE(ROUND(100 * (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM listings x WHERE x.city = l.city AND x.nightly_price < l.nightly_price)
                      / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM listings y WHERE y.city = l.city) - 1, 0), 1), 0) AS price_percentile
FROM listings l
ORDER BY l.city, l.nightly_price, l.title;

traps.explain_md: CUME_DIST counts the row itself and its ties, so nobody scores 0 and tied listings jump higher.
traps.sql:
SELECT city, title, nightly_price,
       ROUND(CUME_DIST() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY nightly_price) * 100, 1) AS price_percentile
FROM listings
ORDER BY city, nightly_price, title;

problems.title: Top quarter of titles
problems.statement_md: A Netflix-style home page features the top quarter of the catalogue by `completion_pct` (the share of viewers who finish a title), but tied titles must be treated alike: a group of titles with the same completion is either entirely featured or not at all, and a group is featured only if every member sits within the best 25% of the catalogue (counting the group itself). Return `title_id`, `title`, `completion_pct` for the featured titles, ordered by `completion_pct` descending, then `title_id`.

tables.name: catalogue
tables.description_md: One row per title; there are 12 titles.

hints_md: A quarter of 12 titles is 3, but two titles tie for the 3rd and 4th place.
For each title ask what fraction of the catalogue completes at least as well as it does, itself included.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Top x% with ties at the boundary. The edge case is the whole point of the question.

**Shape:** For each title compute the cumulative share of the catalogue from the top down, including its tied peers, and keep those whose share is within the limit.

**Syntax:** `CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY x DESC)` = rows ahead plus all peers, divided by total rows, so tied rows always get the same value. `PERCENT_RANK` and `NTILE` treat the boundary differently.

**Trap:** NTILE(4) cuts the tied pair in half; PERCENT_RANK <= 0.25 lets the whole tied group in because it measures rows strictly ahead.

**Interview follow-up:** How would you return exactly the top 25% of rows, ignoring ties? (Number the rows and compare to a quarter of the count.)

solutions.label: CUME_DIST
solutions.explain_md: The cumulative share counts the whole tied group, so a group that crosses the 25% line gets a value above it and is excluded together.
solutions.sql:
WITH d AS (
  SELECT title_id, title, completion_pct,
         CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY completion_pct DESC) AS share_at_or_above
  FROM catalogue
)
SELECT title_id, title, completion_pct
FROM d
WHERE share_at_or_above <= 0.25
ORDER BY completion_pct DESC, title_id;

solutions.label: Correlated count
solutions.explain_md: A title qualifies when the number of titles completing at least as well is at most a quarter of the catalogue.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.title_id, c.title, c.completion_pct
FROM catalogue c
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM catalogue x WHERE x.completion_pct >= c.completion_pct) * 4 <= (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM catalogue)
ORDER BY c.completion_pct DESC, c.title_id;

traps.explain_md: NTILE(4) splits the tied pair across the quarter boundary and keeps one of them.
traps.sql:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT title_id, title, completion_pct,
         NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY completion_pct DESC, title_id) AS q
  FROM catalogue
)
SELECT title_id, title, completion_pct FROM t WHERE q = 1
ORDER BY completion_pct DESC, title_id;

traps.explain_md: PERCENT_RANK looks only at rows strictly ahead, so the whole tied pair passes the 0.25 test.
traps.sql:
WITH p AS (
  SELECT title_id, title, completion_pct,
         PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY completion_pct DESC) AS pr
  FROM catalogue
)
SELECT title_id, title, completion_pct FROM p WHERE pr <= 0.25
ORDER BY completion_pct DESC, title_id;

problems.title: Top three with a tie-breaker
problems.statement_md: An online shooter ranks runs on each map by `score` (higher is better) and, for equal scores, by `clear_seconds` (faster is better). Runs that are equal on both score and clear time share a place and the next place is skipped. Return the runs in places 1 to 3 of each map: `map_name`, `player`, `score`, `clear_seconds`, `place`, ordered by `map_name`, then `place`, then `player`.
hints_md: The ordering inside the window has two keys, pointing in different directions.
Place 3 is shared by CleoCrit and DevDash on Neon Docks; check what that does to the places after them.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Ranking on a composite key. Real leaderboards always have a tie-breaker.

**Shape:** Rank inside each map using both keys, the stronger key first, then keep places up to three in an outer query.

**Syntax:** `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY a DESC, b ASC)` compares rows on the whole key list: rows are peers only if every listed key is equal. Each key has its own direction.

**Trap:** Ranking on score alone gives tied scores the same place and ignores the time; putting the time first makes speed beat score.

**Interview follow-up:** How would you break a complete tie by earliest submission, so places are unique? (Add the id as a final key and switch to ROW_NUMBER.)

solutions.label: RANK on two keys
solutions.explain_md: Runs are peers only when both score and time match, so RANK gives faster runs the better place and shares places only on a full tie.
solutions.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT map_name, player, score, clear_seconds,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY map_name ORDER BY score DESC, clear_seconds ASC) AS place
  FROM ranked_runs
)
SELECT map_name, player, score, clear_seconds, place
FROM ranked
WHERE place <= 3
ORDER BY map_name, place, player;

solutions.label: Correlated count
solutions.explain_md: The place is one plus the number of runs on the same map that are strictly better on score, or equal on score and faster.
solutions.sql:
SELECT map_name, player, score, clear_seconds, place
FROM (
  SELECT r.map_name, r.player, r.score, r.clear_seconds,
         1 + (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ranked_runs x
              WHERE x.map_name = r.map_name
                AND (x.score > r.score OR (x.score = r.score AND x.clear_seconds < r.clear_seconds))) AS place
  FROM ranked_runs r
) t
WHERE place <= 3
ORDER BY map_name, place, player;

traps.explain_md: Ranking by score alone ignores the clear time: tied scores share a place and the faster run gets no credit.
traps.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT map_name, player, score, clear_seconds,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY map_name ORDER BY score DESC) AS place
  FROM ranked_runs
)
SELECT map_name, player, score, clear_seconds, place
FROM ranked WHERE place <= 3
ORDER BY map_name, place, player;

traps.explain_md: Putting clear_seconds first lets speed beat score.
traps.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT map_name, player, score, clear_seconds,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY map_name ORDER BY clear_seconds ASC, score DESC) AS place
  FROM ranked_runs
)
SELECT map_name, player, score, clear_seconds, place
FROM ranked WHERE place <= 3
ORDER BY map_name, place, player;

problems.title: Longest login streak
problems.statement_md: A bank's mobile app team wants to reward loyal customers. For each customer, find the longest run of consecutive calendar days on which they logged in to the app. A customer may log in several times on the same day; that day counts once. Return `customer_id` and `longest_streak` (in days) for every customer who logged in at least once, ordered by `longest_streak` descending, then `customer_id`.

tables.name: app_logins
tables.description_md: One row per login event; customers can log in several times a day.

hints_md: A streak is a block of dates that are consecutive: think about what stays constant for dates in one block when you subtract a counter that grows by one per row.
Duplicate logins on one day break that counter, so remove them before numbering.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Gaps and islands (streaks). The interviewer's favourite hard window question.

**Shape:** Reduce to one row per customer and day, number each customer's days, and subtract that number of days from the date: consecutive days share the same result. Group by that result to get each streak's length, then take the longest per customer.

**Syntax:** `DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL n DAY)` moves a date back by n days; `COUNT(*)` per island gives its length.

**Trap:** Numbering raw login rows: a second login on the same day uses up a number, so a real streak splits or merges. Counting distinct days per customer ignores gaps entirely.

**Interview follow-up:** How would you find the customer's current streak ending today? (Keep only the island whose last date is today.)

solutions.label: Date minus ROW_NUMBER
solutions.explain_md: After de-duplicating to one row per day, date minus row number is constant inside a streak, so grouping on it measures each streak.
solutions.sql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, login_date FROM app_logins
), islands AS (
  SELECT customer_id, login_date,
         DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY login_date) DAY) AS grp
  FROM days
), streaks AS (
  SELECT customer_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS len
  FROM islands
  GROUP BY customer_id, grp
)
SELECT customer_id, MAX(len) AS longest_streak
FROM streaks
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY longest_streak DESC, customer_id;

solutions.label: LAG flag and running sum
solutions.explain_md: Flag each day that does not continue the previous day, then a running sum of flags labels the streaks.
solutions.sql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, login_date FROM app_logins
), flagged AS (
  SELECT customer_id, login_date,
         CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(login_date, LAG(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY login_date)) = 1 THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS is_new
  FROM days
), islands AS (
  SELECT customer_id, login_date,
         SUM(is_new) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY login_date) AS grp
  FROM flagged
), streaks AS (
  SELECT customer_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS len
  FROM islands
  GROUP BY customer_id, grp
)
SELECT customer_id, MAX(len) AS longest_streak
FROM streaks
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY longest_streak DESC, customer_id;

traps.explain_md: Numbering raw login rows lets a repeated login shift the counter, so customer 1's streak is mis-measured.
traps.sql:
WITH islands AS (
  SELECT customer_id, login_date,
         DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY login_date) DAY) AS grp
  FROM app_logins
), streaks AS (
  SELECT customer_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS len
  FROM islands
  GROUP BY customer_id, grp
)
SELECT customer_id, MAX(len) AS longest_streak
FROM streaks
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY longest_streak DESC, customer_id;

traps.explain_md: Counting distinct login days ignores the gaps between streaks.
traps.sql:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(DISTINCT login_date) AS longest_streak
FROM app_logins
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY longest_streak DESC, customer_id;
